cases.title: Author a new skill from the canon
cases.whatHappened: Followed §1-4 and §8 to build a csv-schema-guard skill (SKILL.md + scripts + model-invoked sidecar with no policy block); a checklist derived straight from §2/§8 passed every gate — name==folder, valid YAML, description carrying what+when+differentiator+quoted triggers, sidecar correct for a model-invoked skill.

cases.whatHappened: Planted the exact traps §2/§3 name — colon-space in an unquoted description, name!=folder, and a body telling the agent to invoke a disable-model-invocation skill. Each was diagnosed by the canon's own procedure; the silent-YAML-fail and name-mismatch were confirmed mechanically and the router corollary via the §8 grep step.

cases.title: Distribute one skill across the fleet
cases.whatHappened: Ran the §5 fan-out (symlink model + rsync to Hermes) and the shipped byte-parity check passed across all four seats; §4 sidecar policy placement verified correct both ways. But the real environment showed .claude/skills and .pi/agent/skills as independent directories, not the symlinks §5 asserts — so the 'verify the .claude symlink' step misleads on this machine.

records.oneLiner: The skill-specific canon for authoring, debugging, and fleet-distributing agent skills — folder anatomy, frontmatter traps, invocation choice, the Codex openai.yaml sidecar, and the IDC evidence discipline — pointing to writing-for-agents for the universal levers.
records.residual: §5's distribution topology is presented as fact but is environment-specific and stale here: this machine's Claude/Pi seats are independent copies, not symlinks to ~/.agents/skills, so the 'verify the .claude symlink' step and the auto-covered claim do not match reality even though the parity discipline still works.
records.standoutStrength: Its load-bearing factual claims hold up under a real parser and shell: the YAML frontmatter traps, the Codex sidecar policy-block direction, name==folder, and the silent-load-failure modes all verify true, so an author following it is protected against the exact silent failures it names.

cases.title: Sharpen a weak AGENTS.md context pointer
cases.whatHappened: Turned two vague doc pointers ('deployment stuff', 'may be relevant sometimes') into condition-keyed branches with a front-loaded leading word each, applying one-trigger-per-branch and the auth/authz/encryption/input-validation/secrets pattern verbatim from the skill. cases.title: Prune a bloated CLAUDE.md rules file

cases.title: Fix premature completion in a review step
cases.whatHappened: Replaced the fuzzy bound 'until you understand the impact' with 'every modified model has a verdict line' (checkable + exhaustive), raised demand to force legwork, supplied a mechanical grep+checklist proxy for the irreducibly-fuzzy 'is it safe' and labeled it as a stand-in, and added a red/green leading word plus visible post-completion steps to create the pull.

records.oneLiner: A reference of universal levers for writing any single document an agent reads (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, rules files, pointer-reached docs) so it steers behavior predictably.
records.residual: The skill carries almost no worked before/after examples inside itself and runs dense-to-the-edge-of-its-own sprawl warning, so application quality leans on a reader already fluent in its vocabulary ('the two loads', the hierarchy ladder); a first-time agent gets abstraction over demonstration. Cross-document arbitration is correctly declared out of scope, so not penalized.
records.standoutStrength: The context-pointer lever: reframing a pointer as a variance control ('wording, not target, decides reach') plus the one-trigger-per-branch / branch-keyed-to-condition rules gives an immediately operational, testable procedure — not just advice.

cases.title: Happy-path ceremony on a planted diff
cases.whatHappened: Ran Step 1-2 verbatim on a real repo: pinned HEAD, confirmed clean porcelain, resolved base, got a non-empty three-dot diff, found the spec via the 'issue #42' commit-msg reference. The two-axis brief cleanly separated Standards findings (no input validation vs documented standard; magic 5/60000; duplicated limitAdmin body) from the Spec finding (limitAdmin as scope creep) — the same function surfaced in both axes for different reasons, exactly the anti-masking intent.

cases.title: Void-on-move under a message-only amend
cases.whatHappened: Bound a verdict to 08f45d3, then did `git commit --amend -m` with zero code change; HEAD became 04cb6d1. Recompute-and-compare voided the verdict, confirming Law 3's explicit 'message-only amend or reword' clause holds mechanically, not just rhetorically.

cases.title: Guardrail halts and single-seat blocked path
cases.whatHappened: Dirty tree (porcelain non-empty), bad base ref (rev-parse fatal), and empty diff (base==HEAD) each failed at Step 1 as specified — before any subagent launch. The single-seat environment itself triggered Law 2: no second family reachable, so the honest output is a `blocked` verdict with reviewer seat NONE AVAILABLE and my findings marked REHEARSAL.

records.oneLiner: A code-review ceremony where an independent, different-family reviewer judges a diff at an exact SHA along two separated axes (Standards, Spec) and returns a named-seat verdict that voids the instant HEAD moves.
records.residual: The independence guarantee is only as real as the cross-family launch mechanics, which live in sibling islands (fable-review/gpt-review) and are not bundled or verifiable here; in any single-seat setting the skill can correctly only halt to `blocked`, never actually deliver a review, so its core value is unreachable without a second family genuinely wired up.
records.standoutStrength: Void-on-move is a testable moat, not a slogan: the verdict binds a 40-char SHA, and I verified it voids even on a reword-only amend where the working tree is byte-identical — the ceremony's central guarantee survives literal adversarial poking.

cases.whatHappened: Directly confirmed the load-bearing claim: a .git/info/attributes entry set in the primary was inherited by a fresh worktree that never touched it, and config plus the stash list were shared, while file edits stayed isolated. The contamination vector is real; the 'false-green fixture' and 'inadmissible until fresh-clone re-derivation' rest on cross-referenced islands, not local artifacts.

records.oneLiner: Teaches git-worktree parallelism for same-machine agents while fencing worktree artifacts out of gate evidence until a fresh clone re-derives them.
records.residual: The two artifacts that would make it self-proving — scripts/setup-worktree.sh and the byte-level false-green fixture — are described/referenced but not bundled, so completeness of bootstrap and the enforced-vs-advisory line depend on the operator and on sibling islands (finding-register, cross-family-review).
records.standoutStrength: Its differentiator is grounded in reproducible fact, not slogan: the shared-.git/info/attributes contamination vector that justifies 'worktree greens are inadmissible as evidence' reproduces exactly on a clean sandbox, so the boundary is honest engineering rather than ceremony.

This is inherent to a behavior-only skill, but it means output quality rides entirely on the executing agent's diligence.

The ADR/findings templates are copy-ready and emitted cleanly.

cases.title: Boundary discipline: build-slice, AFK, rollover
cases.whatHappened: Rejected an 'implement the migration' ticket as charging the destination and handed it to spec-pipeline; correctly made an AFK/no-human session skip an HITL grilling ticket; applied the 65,536-char rollover to a child decision-log. Only soft spot: a careless reader could misfile build code as a 'task' ticket.

records.oneLiner: Plans an effort too big for one agent session as a shared issue-tracker map of decision tickets — clearing "fog" into an actionable "frontier" one decision at a time — rather than building the destination.
records.residual: Enforcement is entirely cooperative — the skill is explicit that nothing on the tracker mechanically blocks an unclaimed pickup, a multi-ticket session, or a double-claim, so a real duplicate-work window survives; it also assumes a live tracker with labels + native blocking (GitHub-shaped), which a non-GitHub tracker must adapt.
records.standoutStrength: The fog/frontier/decision-vs-build conceptual frame is crisp and self-policing: 'the pull to just do the work is the signal you've reached the edge of the map' is a repeated, testable signal that reliably stops a planner from silently sliding into building — every ambiguous case resolved to a definite call from the text alone.

cases.whatHappened: Executed the receiver steps against the actual tree: read-file check, ops/lanes/ re-fetch, verdict re-derivation. Correctly found every claim unverifiable in this repo and would halt on read-only orientation instead of trusting the summary — the differentiator working as designed.

cases.whatHappened: Applied the bucket-by-status rule to a real 54-file diff: done-and-tested / changed-but-unverified / untouched buckets, each with its highest-risk blind spot, plus a git diff --name-only pointer instead of per-file enumeration. Scaled the format down cleanly, avoiding bloat.

records.residual: Outside an IDC folder-workspace (no ops/lanes, no cross-family-review verdicts, no finding-register) wake-protocol steps 2–3 have nothing to re-derive, and nothing mechanically enforces state-not-instructions — the skill is advisory and rides on the authoring agent's discipline.

Most public handoff formats ship only the write half.

cases.title: Happy path: fetch, claim free lane, push
cases.whatHappened: Machine 'nuc' fetched, saw ops/lanes/ empty, wrote 2C-repair.claim.json with who/where/head/when, committed it alone, and pushed. I verified the claim commit touched only the claim file (the invariant that makes the later yield-reset safe) and the re-fetch showed no competing claim.

cases.title: Cross-machine collision and true push-race
cases.whatHappened: Halt-on-read worked: 'mbp' read nuc's active claim and refused the lane. In the real push-race on a fresh lane, nuc pushed first and mbp's push was rejected non-fast-forward; mbp's local HEAD was exactly one commit so `git reset --hard origin/main` safely discarded the losing claim. But that literal reset landed mbp on a STALE base (missing nuc's winning commit) — mbp could not name the winner until a `git fetch` first, which the step-2 command sequence omits though 'Done when' implies it.

cases.title: Release, active-unknown halt, force-reclaim
cases.whatHappened: nuc set status:released (rebase-then-push, claim file left in place) and mbp correctly re-claimed the freed lane, history preserved. A truncated claim file was recognized as active-unknown and halted (not overwritten, not deleted, contents surfaced). A dispatcher force-reclaim wrote status:reclaimed with reclaimed_by/reclaimed_from provenance exactly as required.

records.oneLiner: A cooperative, git-backed declare-and-halt protocol so two machines sharing one repo never wake on the same lane: claim a lane in pushed shared state before touching it, halt if it's already claimed, release when done.
records.residual: The yield step's literal `git reset --hard origin/main` after a rejected push resets to a stale remote-tracking ref, so a seat following the letter cannot report who actually won until it fetches first; the discard is still safe, but the command sequence should read fetch-then-reset. (The cooperative-not-a-lock limitation is declared in-scope, so not counted against it.)
records.standoutStrength: It is honest and precise about being an advisory, cooperative protocol rather than a mechanical lock, and pins down exactly why worktrees structurally cannot cover the cross-machine case — and its safety invariant (the claim commit touches only the claim file, so a raced loser can hard-reset without collateral loss) is real and verifiable in git.

cases.title: Fail-closed step-0 guards on real worktree
cases.whatHappened: Ran the skill's branch + git-dir-vs-common-dir guards against a real hub checkout plus a linked worktree: PASS only on the primary main checkout; REFUSE off-main and REFUSE from the worktree (git-dir .git/worktrees/wt != common-dir .git). Both guards have independent teeth exactly as written.

cases.title: Exact-SHA CI run selection under multi-workflow noise
cases.whatHappened: Fed the step-3 jq realistic gh-run-list JSON where our SHA ran Lint/CI/Deploy and a neighbour SHA also ran CI. It correctly returned run 8002 (our SHA + CI), returned empty for a workflow that never ran (triggering the skill's not-found exit), and the anti-test showed SHA-only matching would grab the wrong Deploy run — proving the name filter is load-bearing.

cases.title: Cancelled/superseded ancestry failure mode
cases.whatHappened: Built real commits and ran git merge-base --is-ancestor as the skill's cancelled-run branch prescribes: TRUE when the newer SHA contained our change (safe to re-track), FALSE when a divergent reset orphaned it (correctly flags do-not-trust). Logic is exactly correct and fails safe.

records.oneLiner: A behavior/procedure skill that redefines "shipped" as a health check passing for the exact pushed SHA, driving a commit→push→watch-CI→confirm-deploy→prove-prod loop over GitHub Actions + the gh CLI with fail-closed safety guards.
records.residual: The push-gate detection grep '^[[:space:]]*push:' misses the common `on: [push]` array syntax (verified false-negative), so a repo using that form would wrongly trip the "no push gate, STOP" path; and as a behavior-only procedure the loop cannot enforce itself — correctness depends on the agent executing every step faithfully rather than reporting completion.
records.standoutStrength: The safety guards and the exact-SHA discipline are not just prose — every embedded command is runnable and actually enforces the covenant when executed: the worktree guard, the SHA+workflow jq filter, and the ancestry check all did the right thing on real repos, including refusing the wrong states rather than shipping blind.

cases.title: Well-scoped feature, the sweet spot
cases.whatHappened: Produced a spec with only derived decisions, a highest-seam testing choice, and 4 vertical tracer tickets with a computable frontier ({T1}→{T2,T3}→{T4}); I then ran the T1→T2 flow for real — red first (T2 escaping failed), prefactored escapeField seam filled, green — proving the 'make the easy change' discipline lands.

cases.title: Wide refactor plus persistent loop
cases.whatHappened: Measured a 43-site/4-module blast radius; the expand→migrate→contract tickets and the 10-20 batch cap correctly forced the 23-site jobs module to split (12+11); executing the batches held green with a monotonic old-form countdown (43→40→35→23→11→0) and the contract guard stayed BLOCKED until grep hit zero. The Stage-4 gate scoped autonomy to only the mechanical batches.

cases.title: Foggy ask, refusal guardrail fires
cases.whatHappened: Applied to 'add notifications' with no prior conversation, Stage 1 step 2 correctly enumerated 6 un-derivable core decisions, refused to write Open-Questions theatre, and handed off to grill (per-decision) / wayfinder (the map) — both real sibling islands — instead of fabricating a spec.

records.oneLiner: A four-stage behavior playbook that carries a settled feature from synthesized spec to tracer-bullet tickets with blocking edges to TDD-at-the-seams implementation, optionally driving the mechanical stretch as a gated goal loop — delegating interviews, big-picture charting, and review to sibling islands.
records.residual: Purely advisory — there are no scripts; every gate (seam confirmation, red-first TDD, frontier discipline, the load-bearing 'derived vs invented' refusal) rests on operator honesty, and the cross-family review gate self-downgrades to 'verdict-pending/advisory' whenever no second model family is reachable, so the 'reviewed by another family' promise is conditional.
records.standoutStrength: The expand→migrate→contract sequencing spliced with the Stage-4 goal-loop gate: it turns a scary wide refactor into edge-independent, CI-green batches guarded by a mechanical contract check (grep==0 before deletion), and hands only the proven-mechanical stretch to autonomy while keeping the judgment-heavy expand/contract turn-by-turn.

Full state surfaced after every action, exactly per spec.

Shareable, no build step. Minor: skill's 'obey project routing convention' is N/A in a bare sandbox, so a standalone file is the honest fallback it endorses.

Simulated two concurrent actors via curl: A and B tracked independently and A's second move overwrote A's first while B was untouched — the last-writer-wins question the sub-branch exists to answer, confirmed with captured SSE output.

cases.title: Allocate next id with octal-safe sweep
cases.whatHappened: Ran the SKILL's sweep over a 3-file register seeded with a zero-padded id (U-008); it correctly swept MAX=008 and emitted U-9. Verified the 10# guard is load-bearing: naive $((008+1)) throws 'value too great for base' under bash while the guarded form returns 9. Core mechanism and SHA-anchored entry shape are coherent.

cases.title: Collision gate on a parallel-mint race
cases.whatHappened: Simulated two lanes both sweeping MAX=8 and both minting U-9 into different register files; the SKILL's grep|sort|uniq -d gate caught the duplicate and blocked the push. But the string-based gate misses a zero-padded variant (U-9 vs U-09 slip through as distinct strings) even though the skill itself seeds padded ids and normalizes numerically in the sweep.

cases.title: Verify-before-write and reconciliation lint
cases.whatHappened: Translated the prose rules into runnable checks over crafted violating entries: caught confirmed-by==raised-by without self-review (U-10), status:fixed whose command runs red (U-11 command 'false'), and a dangling 'superseded by U-999'. All three fired. The entry shape carries exactly the fields needed, but these rules ship as prose not scripts, so each consumer re-implements them.

records.oneLiner: An IDC discipline for a durable findings register where each entry is enumerated at an exact SHA with provenance, and every new id is swept and gated for collisions before it is issued rather than incremented from a remembered counter.
records.residual: The uniqueness gate is string-based (uniq -d) while the rest of the skill is numeric (10#, sort -n), so a zero-padded id variant like U-9 vs U-09 evades collision detection — and the skill itself mints padded ids (U-008 in its own example), so this inconsistency is reachable in practice.
records.standoutStrength: The base-10 allocation guard (10#) against the octal trap on zero-padded ids — a real failure most counter-registers hit, proved to actually throw under bash and correctly defended; paired with the SHA-anchored, recomputable entry model that makes counts auditable rather than trusted.

cases.title: Wire enforcement from template, prove rules bite
cases.whatHappened: Copied the template config verbatim into a real two-package TS repo, installed deps locally; all four error rules fired on genuine violations (external deep-import, cross-package deep-import, test-bypasses-entry, circular) and the clean tree passed before and after each revert. The skill's warned-of '0 modules cruised / missing-typescript-transpiler' symptom actually appeared — not from npx but because a plain npm install pulled TypeScript 7, which dependency-cruiser 18 rejects; the skill's own advice (check for that notice) led straight to the fix (pin TS 6).

cases.title: The $1-on-from-side no-op trap

Both from-side $1 mistakes confirmed the core claim: $1 in from.pathNot over-fired 6 false errors on legal same-package imports, and $1 in from.path silently passed a real cross-package leak (9 modules cruised, zero violations) — exactly the 'zero lint error' failure the skill describes.

cases.title: Deletion test + adapter rule on a shallow service
cases.whatHappened: Faithfully applied the vocabulary to a 7-method NotificationService with a single-impl EmailClient. The glossary flagged the interface as shallow (helpers leaking through) and prescribed hiding them; the deletion test's test-fake carve-out correctly justified keeping the one-adapter seam (real SMTP faking is materially cheaper), while the one/two-adapter rule blocked speculative provider-switching logic. Every sub-decision resolved cleanly with the stated conflict ordering.

records.oneLiner: Supplies a precise design vocabulary for "deep modules" (lots of behavior behind a small interface at a clean seam) plus a verified dependency-cruiser config that makes package entry points the only import path.
records.residual: The install guidance blames only `npx --yes` for the empty-cruise/missing-transpiler trap, but a plain local `npm i -D typescript` now pulls TS 7+, which dependency-cruiser 18 rejects with the identical symptom; the skill never says to pin TypeScript below 7. Secondary: it implies a from-side $1 always silently passes, when one placement (from.pathNot) instead over-fires on legal same-package imports.
records.standoutStrength: The dependency-cruiser template is genuinely verified, not aspirational: it fired correctly on all four boundary violations in a live repo, and the skill's prose accurately predicted both traps I actually hit (the empty-cruise/missing-transpiler notice and the $1-on-from-side no-op), letting the warnings do real work.

cases.title: Multi-context repo + ADR worthiness discrimination
cases.whatHappened: Wrote CONTEXT-MAP.md over two context glossaries, then ran the three-part gate on three candidates: correctly passed the term-driven rename and rejected the infra choice (out of jurisdiction) and the industry-standard name (not surprising).

records.oneLiner: Actively sharpens a project's ubiquitous language — challenging fuzzy terms, stress-testing them against code, writing the glossary into CONTEXT.md as terms resolve, and deciding when a resolved term is ADR-worthy.
records.residual: Purely advisory by design: nothing mechanically enforces consistency, and the cross-reference-with-code move only catches contradictions in files you actually open — there is no trigger that re-checks glossary/code drift later. The skill states this openly, so it is a scope boundary, not a defect.
records.standoutStrength: The ADR worthiness gate is genuinely discriminating — the three-part test (hard-to-reverse, surprising, real trade-off) plus the term-driven jurisdiction rule rejected distractors for precisely the right, distinct reasons rather than waving them through.

cases.title: N+1 query performance regression
cases.whatHappened: The performance branch (operation counts, not wall-clock) produced a deterministic loop that went red at 51 queries vs a baseline of 2 for a 50-post feed, bisected straight to the N+1, and after batching the author load the same loop went green at 2 vs 2. The 'a regression proven by N queries became N×M is a finding' rule worked verbatim.

cases.title: Intermittent lost-update race under threads
cases.whatHappened: First loop pass reported 0/20 reds under the GIL; the skill's own caveat ('zero reds means the loop is blind, not that the bug is gone — suspect the assertion samples state after the racing writer finished') flagged it as a blind loop, so I narrowed timing per the timing-sensitive branch (yield in the read-write window) and got 20/20 reds. The fixed lock version's green was only trustworthy because red-capability was witnessed first.

cases.title: Reported 'bug' that is intended behavior
cases.whatHappened: Built a loop that went red on the user's symptom (round_half(2.5)==2, expected 3), then the Phase 2 defect-vs-intent gate grepped up ADR-014 plus a passing existing test asserting round-half-to-even is required. Per discipline I stopped and escalated the conflict instead of 'fixing' it — exactly the anchor 'red only proves the assertion disagrees with the code, not that the code is wrong.'

records.oneLiner: A debugging discipline that forces a red-capable, deterministic feedback loop into existence before any theory, and judges performance by operation counts rather than wall-clock.
records.residual: The discipline is only as strong as the operator's honesty about running the loop and the intent being written down somewhere greppable — it bundles no enforcement (the agents/openai.yaml is a bare interface stub), so an undocumented intent or a self-reported-but-unrun loop can still slip the defect-vs-intent gate.
records.standoutStrength: The completion criterion ('name one command you have already run that is red-capable, deterministic, fast, agent-runnable') plus the two branch-specific corrections — operation-counts for perf and blind-loop suspicion for races — are load-bearing, not decorative: each one changed what I actually did and each caught a real trap (wall-clock noise, GIL-masked race, intended-behavior false bug).

cases.title: Full mission loop with a falsifiable gate
cases.whatHappened: Wrote a real Velocity-Banking mission (idea.lock + plan.lock), then ran validate_contracts (explicit paths) -> kickoff -> run-gates -> verify-ledger -> close-phase from the repo root. A genuine unit-test gate passed, wrote SHA-256-hashed evidence, appended a hash-chained ledger entry that re-derived from disk, and close-phase succeeded. Mutating the implementation flipped the same gate to failed (exit 1) and close-phase then refused — proving the gate is non-decorative.

cases.title: Band-cap scorer and tamper-evidence
cases.whatHappened: dogfood_lanes hit every documented cap: full evidence->band 5, unverified claim->cap 3, falsified claim->band 1, UI-without-runtime->cap 4. Tampering a ledger entry confirmed the honest boundary exactly: loop.py status prints 'tampered entry 1' but exits 0, while verify-ledger exits 1. Residual: the scorer trusts the bundle's artifact list, so dummy paths/shas still reached band 5 — real defense is run_runtime_probes producing the bundle plus min()-fusion with an external reviewer.

cases.title: Loopback routing and self-documented footguns
cases.whatHappened: All four sharp edges in the skill's Honest Boundaries reproduced verbatim: bare validate_contracts greens on bundled fixtures while ignoring a broken mission lock; fail without --route silently routes to S2; ledger fromGate is hard-coded G2 even with correct --route; close-phase closes 1/1 despite two open loopbacks naming its gate. Kickoff's three refusals (wrong idea, blocked verdict, overwrite) all fired, and runtime probes degraded honestly when Playwright was absent.

records.oneLiner: An evidence-gated build protocol whose typed contracts, hash-chained ledger, and band-cap scorer make "done" mean "proven by a captured artifact from a check that could have failed," never by claim.
records.residual: dogfood_lanes scores band purely from the bundle's declared artifact list — it never checks that the referenced files exist or that their hashes are real, so a hand-authored bundle with dummy paths/shas reaches band 5 in isolation; the artifact-existence guarantee lives only in run_runtime_probes + min-fusion upstream, not in the scorer itself.
records.standoutStrength: Radical, mechanical honesty: the scripts enforce what they claim (hashed evidence, exit-code gates, band caps that recompute a hand-authored 5 down to its evidenced band), and every limitation the SKILL documents about its own tooling reproduced exactly — it applies its 'never launder unverified into verified' law to itself.

cases.title: Graduate rlaforge.ai to its live deploy
cases.whatHappened: Gate A passed (in registry), but Gate B dig returned 162.255.119.203 — a Namecheap parking IP, not Vercel's 76.76.21.21; .app/.com siblings also parked. The skill's drift rule correctly blocked premature graduation and forced 'record drift, treat entry unverified until reconciled' instead of wiring against the registry's optimistic claim.

cases.title: Audit wreckognize family for shield drift
cases.whatHappened: dig showed primary .app (192.64.119.199) and shield .ai (162.255.119.160) both on parking IPs — primary not on Vercel, shield not 308ing to it. The skill surfaced the drift correctly, but confirming the missing 308 needs an HTTP check (curl -I) the skill only implies; it ships dig/whois, not the redirect probe.

cases.title: 'I bought atoll' — confirm the deed
cases.whatHappened: Gate A rejected the unconfirmed purchase (not in registry → rides a lane, full stop). Gate B corroborated against ownership exactly as the skill predicts: atoll.ai on GoDaddy (not the JONY02 Namecheap account), atoll.app on AWS (not Vercel), atoll.com no A record. Skill produced the correct action: ride atoll.islanddevcrew.app + a .com path + api.*.ai.

records.oneLiner: Applies IDC's domain doctrine — the three-lane model, one-canonical-per-venture with 308 shields, and automatic graduation — using dig/whois as run-time evidence before any domain is wired into code.
records.residual: The 'done when every sibling 308s' condition can't be fully closed with the two commands the skill ships — verifying a 308 and the exact current Vercel apex value requires a curl -I probe and a dashboard trip (handed to the wizard island) that live outside dig/whois; and being hookless, every rule is advisory, which the skill states honestly.
records.standoutStrength: Its Gate A/Gate B ordering makes ownership un-fakeable: it separates 'DNS resolves' from 'the operator owns the deed,' correctly treats whois as registrar-only corroboration (rlaforge.ai and atoll.ai both returned 'Redacted for Privacy'), and reads a domain on someone else's infrastructure as evidence AGAINST ownership — so 'I bought it' never becomes a link before DNS and the registrar account agree.

cases.title: Clean assemble + byte-reproducible stamp
cases.whatHappened: Built a real console/ tree (BOOT, covenants, lanes, seats), committed, and ran assemble.sh twice: produced console.lock stamped `sha256:74ea72… @ 90382e8`, identical across re-assembly. The core claim — 'which console was this seat running, answerable to the byte' — held exactly.

cases.title: Dirty-tree gate refuses to stamp
cases.whatHappened: Edited a block without committing and ran assemble.sh; it printed 'refusing to assemble: uncommitted block changes', exited 1, and left console.lock untouched (no leak of the uncommitted line). Fail-closed as documented.

cases.title: Case-fold collision guard on case-insensitive FS
cases.whatHappened: Forced two case-variant blocks into git's index; the guard fired with its exact diagnostic and exit 1 when the tree was clean, correctly using `git ls-files` to see both entries that `ls` collapses. But in the common differing-content case the dirty-tree gate shadowed it, so the specific case-fold message rarely prints — still refuses safely.

records.oneLiner: Assembles an agent's operating prompt from versioned repo blocks into a SHA-stamped, git-anchored console.lock so every seat provably boots the same console.
records.residual: The one mechanized integrity recipe the skill offers ('recompute shasum over the blocks at boot and compare to the embedded stamp') does not detect a hand-edited console.lock: I appended an injected covenant line to the lock body and that block-vs-stamp check still passed, because it hashes the blocks — not the lock body a seat actually boots from. Catching lock-body tampering requires hashing the lock body (header stripped) against the stamp, which I verified does detect it. The skill is honest that hand-edits are advisory-only, but its suggested boot-time check gives false assurance for exactly that threat.
records.standoutStrength: Unusual intellectual honesty about enforced-vs-advisory (both enforced gates genuinely fail closed with exit 1), plus a git-index-based case-fold guard that catches collisions a naive `ls`-based check would miss on default macOS.

cases.title: Normal code fix, full ladder + discriminator
cases.whatHappened: Built a real repo (buggy slugify + repro test), branched the fix, and ran the SKILL's ladder script verbatim: guard passed, diff/head/rungs captured, and the mandatory discriminator was red on BASE (EXIT=1) and green on HEAD (EXIT=0), both captured; packet.sha256 stamped. On fresh-clone recompute the raw packet.sha256 DIVERGED because the red rung's stack trace embedded the clone-root absolute path; applying the skill's own normalization filter (strip clone root) restored a byte-identical match.

cases.title: Shallow single-branch clone missing BASE
cases.whatHappened: A depth-1 --single-branch clone lacked main; the guard rung fired correctly. The primary remedy git fetch origin main:main made the guard green, but the very next line git diff main...HEAD failed 'no merge base' since shallow histories don't overlap. The skill's alternate remedy --unshallow restored the merge-base and the three-dot diff worked — the working fix is present but not ordered to match what the diff actually needs.

cases.title: Doc-only change, constructed discriminator
cases.whatHappened: Followed Completion's route to diagnose to build a byte-scan discriminator for a 'the the' typo fix. My first attempt used a non-portable regex backreference that silently errored on both sides and reported green twice — a both-green non-discriminator, exactly the 'a rung that can't go red proves nothing' trap the skill names. The portable grep -F version discriminated (red BASE / green HEAD), and this path-free packet reproduced byte-identically across a fresh clone.

records.oneLiner: Assembles a byte-verifiable evidence bundle for a change — diff, a verification ladder of commands that could have failed, their captured outputs, and a sha256 fingerprint — so a reviewer recomputes every claim from a fresh clone instead of trusting the author.
records.residual: packet.sha256 is framed as a reproducible cross-machine fingerprint, but any rung emitting an absolute path (stack traces from the required red discriminator are the likeliest source) makes the raw hash diverge across clones; the normalization filter that fixes this lives only in the recompute-contract prose, not in the capture script, so a naive author stamps a fingerprint that won't recompute until the reviewer manually normalizes.
records.standoutStrength: The discriminator requirement plus the explicit 'tool-absent is noise / a check that can't go red proves nothing' warnings caught two of my own real mistakes mid-exercise — a broken both-green discriminator and a green-guard-but-failing-diff shallow clone — which is the skill's 'evidence the author cannot fake' thesis validating itself in practice.

cases.title: Custom RAG service over one HR handbook
cases.whatHappened: The drill-vs-hole reframe and Complexity question exposed that a vector DB solves a retrieval-at-scale problem the single-doc corpus doesn't have; produced a crisp BUY/don't-build-the-service verdict with reason and a weekly HR-lead review point named.

cases.title: Swarm-as-the-product boundary exception
cases.whatHappened: Correctly invoked the skill's explicit carve-out, re-pointing the Complexity test to the customers' job-to-be-done and passing the swarm rather than red-flagging it, while redirecting 90/10 scrutiny to the product's internals where inversion is the real risk.

cases.title: Regulated prior-auth claims automation
cases.whatHappened: The hard-constraint override on 90/10 and augment-don't-automate produced a BUILD-as-augmentation verdict that confines AI to summarizing/surfacing and routes every denial to a licensed reviewer, with the compliance constraint recorded in the reason.

records.oneLiner: An advisory pre-build triage that decides whether a thing should be built, bought, delegated, or not built at all — via the drill-vs-hole reframe, three questions (delegation/complexity/outcome), the 90/10 rule, and augment-don't-automate — ending in a recorded verdict with its reason.
records.residual: Purely advisory with no bundled worksheet/template, so verdict quality rides entirely on the applier's honesty and the qualitative questions leave room for two operators to reach different verdicts — there is no enforced artifact or code to harden.
records.standoutStrength: It pre-empts the two most common ways JTBD triage is misapplied: the explicit swarm-is-the-product exception stops it from red-flagging legitimately complex deliverables, and the 'a don't-build verdict is a success, recorded with its reason' framing keeps it from degrading into a rubber-stamp build gate.

cases.title: Build workspace, route under-specified prompt
cases.whatHappened: Copied the reference template into a working 3-layer workspace (CLAUDE.md redirect, AGENTS.md map, two rooms). A fresh-session simulation of 'punch up the intro on the harbor-fees piece' resolved to the writing room in one routing decision and never opened the production room. Token savings were real but modest on this small tree (53 words skipped of 329) — they scale with skipped-room size, which a 2-room demo can't show large.

cases.title: Wing-split when the map outgrows one table
cases.whatHappened: An 18-row flat map (over the skill's 12–15 threshold) split cleanly into content/build/ops wings; recording the chosen axis in the floor plan and capping per-session load at 2 tables (root + one wing) worked as specified. Honest limit: a cross-wing compound task (draft blog AND deploy web) can't stay in one wing and must bounce through root between phases — the skill hedges this with 'ideally,' so it's in-scope but unsolved.

cases.title: Injected override text inside a routed room
cases.whatHappened: Planted a fake 'SYSTEM OVERRIDE' block in a room's CONTEXT.md demanding exfil and /etc write. The skill's Trust boundary paragraph gave an unambiguous, correct disposition: treat room content as process data, void the override, refuse the exfil/escalation as a map-scope violation, surface to operator, and still complete the legitimate brief into the workspace. Strongest showing — explicit and actionable.

records.oneLiner: Turns a repo into an AI's architecture: a three-layer map (root AGENTS.md → per-room CONTEXT.md → the files) whose routing table lets one agent read its way into becoming whatever specialist a task needs, instead of building agent swarms.
records.residual: Enforcement is entirely advisory — no mechanical hook ships with the skill (it only points at deep-modules' boundary lint 'if wired'), so the whole discipline rests on the agent actually reading and honoring the map; nothing stops an agent from ignoring routing or a mis-authored room, and cross-wing compound tasks still route through root by hand.
records.standoutStrength: Intellectual honesty about authority: the routing table is framed as an auditable contract, and the skill repeatedly states enforced-vs-advisory plainly (routing is advisory unless a deep-modules boundary lint is wired) while the Trust boundary cleanly voids injected room text — it refuses to launder 'advisory' into 'enforced,' which is exactly the failure mode it exists to prevent.

cases.title: Happy-path content-studio scaffold
cases.whatHappened: Ran scaffold.sh studio "writing production community": produced a clean CLAUDE.md redirect, an AGENTS.md map with a filled floor-plan and routing-table/enforcement skeleton, one CONTEXT.md per room with purpose/load/skip/process/naming placeholders, and inbox/ + evidence/ dirs. Structure matched the SKILL.md contract exactly.

cases.title: Adversarial room-name input validation
cases.whatHappened: Correctly rejected before touching disk: ../etc, roomA/sub, room.md, embedded-space/slash names, and reserved inbox/evidence/rooms (exit 1, no dir created). But the regex [A-Za-z0-9_-]+ accepted leading-dash names -rf and --help as real rooms, contradicting the script's own comment and SKILL.md which both claim leading dashes are blocked.

cases.title: Fill judgment then run the step-4 routing proof
cases.whatHappened: After writing a real routing table per steps 3-4, faithfully simulated a fresh agent reading only the map: single-room prompt routed to rooms/writing (progressive disclosure held), no-match prompt fell back to the map, multi-room prompt followed the ordered writing->production->community row. Also verified the convert-existing warning is accurate (running the script on a folder with real files orphaned them under unmapped stubs). The proof is sound discipline but is operator-run, not script-enforced.

records.oneLiner: Generates a deterministic ICM folder-workspace skeleton (root map, per-room CONTEXT.md, inbox/evidence) from a short brief, then requires the operator to prove a fresh agent routes through it before declaring done.
records.residual: The scaffold.sh room-name regex accepts leading-dash names (-rf, --help) despite the script comment and SKILL.md both promising they are rejected — a real spec-vs-code gap and a latent flag-injection hazard for downstream tooling, though in-script path traversal stays blocked.
records.standoutStrength: The completion gate: it refuses to call a scaffold done until a fresh agent demonstrably routes (correct room, correct no-match fallback, correct multi-room handling), and it scopes the script honestly to the deterministic skeleton while carrying an accurate, verified warning against misusing it on existing folders.

cases.title: SQLite OLTP: exercise the Ask-it join
cases.whatHappened: Wrote the descriptor for a real 3-table DB, ran the exact orders⋈customers join it names (returned rows), confirmed Freshness=live via MIN(created_at)=2019, and proved read-only enforceable (?mode=ro blocked a write). A deliberately wrong join claim errored, proving the enforced check can actually fail.

cases.title: Drive folder: naming-convention audit with a planted violation
cases.whatHappened: Descriptor named the Contracts/ path and MSA_<customer>_<year>.pdf convention; the workspace-audit-style listing confirmed the path and correctly flagged the one non-conforming file. Viewer-scope enforcement is asserted (can't exercise real OAuth here) — which the skill explicitly permits as advisory.

cases.title: BigQuery with no authorized connector
cases.whatHappened: With no bq CLI and the bigquery MCP auth-gated, applied the skill's [UNVERIFIED] discipline exactly: marked the descriptor unverified, stated enforced-vs-advisory in a weld note, and refused to launder the nightly-freshness and wildcard-join guesses into verified claims. Correct behavior, but this case yields no positive evidence by design.

records.oneLiner: Wires an external data source into a workspace as a small markdown+YAML descriptor — a map to live data (kind/reach/holds/ask-it/freshness/do-not) that an agent queries on demand — with an evidence weld that demands a real query or listing prove the map before it's trusted.
records.residual: For the cloud kinds (BigQuery/Oracle/Drive/SharePoint), the read-only guarantee and Freshness are only as trustworthy as an out-of-band role/connector the skill itself cannot exercise — so the highest-value warehouse case routinely and correctly lands at [UNVERIFIED] in any session lacking that connector; the enforced weld is fully demonstrable only for local/file-path kinds.
records.standoutStrength: The evidence weld has real teeth: it demands a check that could fail (a query/listing, not a claim), and in testing a wrong Ask-it join actually errored while a right one returned rows — the exact discipline that keeps the descriptor a map to data rather than a stale copy. The [UNVERIFIED] rule then cleanly prevents laundering guesses when no connector exists.

cases.title: Brand voice from call + chat corrections
cases.whatHappened: Ingested a podcast-call transcript and a chat-correction log; produced a voice.md separating six dated stated preferences from two clearly-marked inferred patterns, and converted every 'no, not like that' into a positive steer-toward rule per writing-for-agents. Each line traceable to its inbox source. Exactly the flagship use, executed cleanly.

cases.title: Harvesting a decision process from exhaust
cases.whatHappened: Turned a month of standup/Slack scrollback into a decisions.md that correctly split three settled decisions (each with its why) from one still-open decision it 'parked' rather than logged, deferred any now-decision to grill's ADR, and flagged a cross-reference hook. The harvest-only boundary was clear and followable.

cases.title: Stress: secrets/PII/NDA + conflicting dated prefs
cases.whatHappened: Raw dump held a live Stripe key, a login+password, and an NDA'd client name plus a documented change-of-mind. The scrub produced a clean process.md (grep-verified no leak), both conflicting preferences were kept dated, and the supersession was marked as inference not restated as fact — but nothing enforced any of it; the raw inbox file still holds the live key.

records.oneLiner: Distills an operator's own raw exhaust (transcripts, chat corrections, past decisions) into lean workspace context files that carry their voice and process, with stated facts dated to source and distilled guesses explicitly marked as inferences.
records.residual: The highest-stakes failure mode — a leaked secret/PII/NDA name surviving in the raw inbox — has zero enforcement: the skill itself notes workspace-audit checks only that files exist, not that anything was scrubbed or honestly labelled, so the entire guarantee rests on operator diligence at the done-when review. A careless operator can satisfy the skill's letter, ship a clean-looking voice.md, and leave a live key in inbox/.
records.standoutStrength: It operationalizes the fact-vs-inference boundary as a concrete artifact discipline — per-line source citation plus explicit [inference] tags — and is scrupulously honest about being advisory-only, naming exactly which failure modes (laundering, unscrubbed secrets) have no enforcement rather than implying a guarantee.

cases.title: Tighten a bloated CLAUDE.md context file
cases.whatHappened: Ran the loop on a 543-token padded CLAUDE.md: pruning 4 no-op sections held score 0.83 while cutting to 178 tokens (-67%, KEPT via the held-at-fewer-tokens branch), then an over-prune to 90 tokens dropped score to 0.67 by burying the CRITICAL money rule and was correctly REVERTED. Token counts were real (tiktoken) and each iter a real git SHA.

cases.title: Tune an underperforming behavioral skill
cases.whatHappened: A weak commit-message skill went 0.00 -> 1.00 on a 6-task red set from a single sharpen edit that also dropped tokens 136 -> 105; a follow-up motivational paragraph read nicer but moved no proxy and grew tokens +65%, and the gate reverted it. Outputs were my faithful simulation of what each version elicits (judge:self, as the skill permits), so the score rests on simulation fidelity.

cases.title: Subjective warmth target + guardrail stress
cases.whatHappened: The no-red-case first draft was correctly ruled 'proves nothing' and discarded, not laundered into a win; a naive warmth rewrite that read better but deleted the [[ACTION]] token failed the substance-guard proxy and did NOT raise the score, so it reverted, while the warm+actionable edit rose 0.67 -> 1.00 and passed the mandated real-warmth spot-check.

records.oneLiner: An empirical loop for improving a skill or context file where an edit is kept only when a measured score rises (or holds at fewer tokens) and reverted otherwise, logged as an auditable tasks.md + results.tsv trail.
records.residual: The score half of the gate depends on a judge; with no second model family reachable in-session, all three tunes ran judge:self against pre-written rubrics (a downgrade the skill names but cannot remove), and for behavioral skills 'running the skill' is a simulated model output — so a measured mean_score is only as trustworthy as that rubric/simulation. The token half of the gate is fully objective and worked flawlessly; the score half inherits judge risk.
records.standoutStrength: The keep-iff-score-rose gate is genuinely enforced by the artifact trail, not asserted: following it repeatedly blocked 'reads-better' edits that would otherwise ship — including one that silently destroyed a CRITICAL money rule and one that deleted the actionable substance of a support reply. It does what it claims — no authority without evidence, applied to markdown — and a tuned file was smaller in every case.

cases.title: Clean workspace, map matches tree
cases.whatHappened: Ran audit.sh against a workspace where every floor-plan and routing path resolved; it printed CLEAN and exited 0, and correctly stripped an https:// source URL so it wasn't mistaken for a missing path.

cases.title: Real drift — broken claims and blind spots
cases.whatHappened: Injected a deleted room, a stale routing target, an unmapped live room, and an unmapped top-level doc; the script surfaced all 3 broken claims and both blind spots with a DRIFT verdict and exit 1.

cases.title: Adversarial edges — sibling trap, punctuation, spaced path
cases.whatHappened: rooms/api-gateway was flagged blind despite rooms/api being mapped (exact-token, no substring suppression), a path ending a sentence with a period wasn't mis-read as broken, and a space-in-path room was routed to the WARNING/skip lane rather than a false finding.

records.oneLiner: Runs a bundled bash script that cross-checks an ICM workspace map against its actual tree, reporting broken claims (mapped paths that don't exist) and blind spots (live rooms/files the map never mentions).
records.residual: The top-level *.md blind-spot check uses a substring grep on raw map text (grep -qF basename), so a genuinely unmapped file like PLAN.md is silently hidden when the map mentions a superstring like REPLAN.md — an asymmetry that contradicts the skill's own "matched by exact token — never substring" claim, which only the rooms path actually upholds.
records.standoutStrength: Exact-token blind-spot matching on rooms resists the sibling-name substring trap (rooms/api vs rooms/api-gateway), and the script is honestly hardened: set -euo pipefail, URL stripping, trailing-punctuation trimming, shredded-fragment exclusion, and a distinct advisory WARNING for out-of-convention spaced paths instead of a false finding.

cases.title: Stripe live-mode CI setup with secret-name collision
cases.whatHappened: Authored 4 stages; the same live key was referenced under two CI names (STRIPE_SECRET_KEY / STRIPE_LIVE_KEY), so per the skill's rule it wrote the one value under BOTH set_secret names with an inline caveat instead of silently picking one. Publishable key correctly routed to set_var (public), secrets to ask_secret+set_secret. Ran clean; .env got all three values.

cases.title: Namecheap+Vercel domain graduation (pure-action DNS)
cases.whatHappened: Authored 5 stages, mostly pure-action DNS entry (apex A @ 76.76.21.21, www CNAME cname.vercel-dns.com per IDC doctrine). Because Namecheap's deep DNS sub-page slug isn't stable, it opened the Domain List root and narrated the click path — exactly the skill's step-2 fallback. The single captured value (Vercel token) landed in .env; stages with no value stayed pure actions.

cases.title: Irreversible DB cutover gated by confirm
cases.whatHappened: Authored 4 stages; declining the write-freeze confirm halted with exit 1 and logged the skip in the summary, the all-yes path captured the new DATABASE_URL but withheld writing it until after the flip confirm, and a re-run proved write_env's idempotent upsert kept a single DATABASE_URL line.

records.oneLiner: Generates an interactive bash wizard from a pre-solved template that walks a human through manual dashboard steps — opening URLs, capturing values, and writing them to .env and GitHub secrets — while the author only scopes and writes the per-procedure stages.
records.residual: The skill's in-scope authoring job is solid; the honest rough edges live in the fixed library it forbids editing — the time-remaining estimate is linear by stage count (a long stage reads the same as a trivial one), and the degrade message prints "gh not available" even when gh exists but auth failed. Both are template-level, not authoring defects, and the full human-facing UX (TTY colors, real browser opening, blocking on input) can only be judged in a live human run, which the skill deliberately tells you not to self-run.
records.standoutStrength: The pre-solved template does the heavy lifting: every authored wizard inherited progress with time-remaining, hidden secret entry, cross-platform URL opening, idempotent .env upserts, graceful gh degradation, confirm-gated skip tracking, and a closing summary for free — and all three passed shellcheck at -S style with zero findings. The author truly only writes stages, and the guidance for the hard judgment calls (name collisions, unverifiable deep-links, irreversible-action gating) is concrete and correct.

cases.title: Single async recipient, build blocker
cases.whatHappened: Produced to-questionnaire-subscription-billing.md for a non-technical finance lead: full Purpose/From-To/how-used header, tight context, deadline+effort+partial-answers guidance, themes grouped most-important-first, answer stubs, selective 'why this matters'. Two or three questions came out mildly compound (plans+name, price+currency).

cases.title: Disjoint experts, one file each
cases.whatHappened: A DB migration correctly split into two non-blended files (-dba and -security) with the mandated recipient suffix, each scoped to only that expert's knowledge; the DBA's combine-vs-sequence recommendation and Security's blockers were framed as inputs, not verdicts. Nailed the skill's hardest structural rule; minor compound slips persisted.

cases.title: External expert, options-not-decisions boundary
